tagline: Mining routes became a mountain drive with gravel at its heart
intro: Mountain Loop links Granite Falls and Darrington through river valleys and glacier-clad peaks in Washington’s Cascades. The Forest Service describes this National Forest Scenic Byway, designated in 1991, through its abandoned claims, former boomtowns and mountain scenery. Pavement gives way to a single-lane gravel middle section, and lingering snow at Barlow Pass usually limits the full drive to late spring through fall.

The route’s beginnings lie in the mining traffic of 1891, when wagon roads opened access to Monte Cristo. Mining interests funded a road from Silverton over Barlow Pass to join the Sauk wagon road. Loggers and the Civilian Conservation Corps later developed the road. Highway construction ran from 1936 to 1941. The CCC work connected ranger stations at Granite Falls and Darrington and opened backcountry to logging and recreation. Flood damage later interrupted the connection: a 2003 flood and subsequent windstorms kept the highway closed until its reopening on June 25, 2008.

From Granite Falls, follow the South Fork Stillaguamish past Verlot and Silverton toward Big Four Mountain. At Barlow Pass the road turns north, becoming gravel Forest Route 20 and following the Sauk toward Darrington. Pavement returns at Whitechuck, with the drive ending at State Route 530. Despite its name, Mountain Loop needs other highways to complete a circuit.

moments.title: Verlot
moments.text: The Civilian Conservation Corps left a visible record beside the South Fork Stillaguamish at Verlot: the buildings of its Public Service Center. Crews built the complex between 1933 and 1942, and the buildings are listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The former ranger station became a visitor center after combining with the Darrington Ranger District. The Forest Service operates the center seasonally, with staff helping visitors plan outings. Its Depression-era architecture survives alongside the road the CCC helped develop. Inside, a museum accompanies maps and information on mountain weather and hiking, giving the old administrative building a visitor role.

moments.title: Big Four Ice Caves
moments.text: Summer meltwater makes the caves at Big Four, flowing beneath avalanche debris piled at the mountain’s north face. That face rises 4,200 feet, and the piles may remain year-round in its permanent shade. The caves can collapse: hikers are advised to stay out of them. The approach has changed too, after river flooding destroyed a major footbridge in 2006. Repairs finished in 2009, but later erosion closed the bridge again in 2019; it reopened in November 2022. Big Four and neighboring Hall Peak are visible from the picnic area where the trail starts.
moments.notice: Big Four Mountain and Hall Peak are visible from the picnic area at the trail’s start.

moments.title: Monte Cristo
moments.text: Monte Cristo’s gold and silver mines drew wagon roads and a railway into these mountains. By 1893 there were 211 mining claims, and a five-level concentrator followed in 1894 to process ore at the townsite. Floods in 1896 and 1897 damaged the railway, and repair bills cut into mining profits. Mining ended in 1907; tourism carried on until the remaining lodge burned in 1983. Few original structures survive. The former town is reached by a separate four-mile route from Barlow Pass, closed to motor vehicles. A preservation association formed in 1983 to save and restore the historical site after the lodge fire.

practical: Verlot: Snow at Barlow Pass usually limits the full drive to late spring through fall. The middle 14 miles are single-lane gravel. (checked 2026-10-11)
